# Preliminaries {#sec-preliminaries}

## Data {#sec-data}

The primary data source for the analysis in @bali2016 is CRSP.
@bali2016 discuss several ways of obtaining CRSP data that applied in 2016 before indicating that they obtained CRSP data in form of SAS data accessed on WRDS servers using SSH [@bali2016, p. 104].

I store the WRDS tables used in this book as Parquet files.

### WRDS tables {#sec-data-vintages}

In 2016, when @bali2016 was published, the canonical form of WRDS data was SAS data files.
For users with WRDS access, [my `wrds2pg` package](https://pypi.org/project/wrds2pg/) can be use to generate Parquet files from SAS data files.
However, I recommend getting data from the WRDS PostgreSQL server instead.

Since 2017, WRDS has provided data through a PostgreSQL database server.
As discussed in @GowDing2024, the SAS data files and the PostgreSQL server can be viewed as [canonical sources of WRDS data](https://iangow.github.io/far_book/parquet-wrds.html#canonical-wrds-data).
For users with WRDS access, [my `db2pq` package](https://pypi.org/project/db2pq/) can be used to generate Parquet files from the PostgreSQL database.
Because using `db2pq` is faster and more robust than using `wrds2pg`, I recommend that you use `db2pq`.

Some books and code repositories reduce the quantity of data retrieved from WRDS by taking subsets of observations or variables.
For example, Tidy Finance [@Scheuch2024] use a script to download a selection of variables from the CRSP daily stock file for subsets of firms in batches.
In contrast, I download the full tables in each case.

While downloading the full WRDS data files used here can take several minutes even with a fast internet connection, I think this is a cost worth bearing for several reasons.
First, many finance researchers will only have access to annual updates and will use the data on a near-daily basis.
So the fixed cost of downloading the data can be amortized over many uses.

Second, managing vintages of data is much easier with the approach used here.
The core `db2pq` function `wrds_update_pq()` used below retains information about the vintage of the data on WRDS and this avoids downloading data that is of the same vintage as the user already has.
Other functions offered by `db2pq` allow the user to retain older vintages and swap them easily if one wants to reproduce data using a specific vintage.

It seems not uncommon for researchers to get a certain set of variables in initial analysis, then need to go back to retrieve additional variables later on when the vintage of the data might be different.
In such cases, a research is confronted with a choice of updating all variables, potentially losing finely balanced results in the process, or just getting data for the additional variables, which introduces potential inconsitencies in the data.
By getting all variables at the outset, this issue is avoided.

Another reason to get the full data files relates to reproducibility.
If your results are generated on a specific subset of a WRDS data file, then I need to get that specific subset to reproduce them.
Because researchers often do not include the code to produce the WRDS data files they use, additional frictions are introduce to reproducibiliy in practice.
In contrast, using `crsp.dsf` produced using `db2pq` will produce exactly the same results as I'd get from using `crsp.dsf` in the PostgreSQL database.

A third approach to managing data avoids storing local data at all.
For example, @GowDing2024 provide code to run analyses in their book using direct connections to the WRDS PostgreSQL server with little or no persistence of data locally.
While this does reduce the initial set-up costs, it introduces issues of performance and even reproducibility that do not seem worth forgoing the modest initial setup costs of the approach used here.^[
    In addition, @GowDing2024 rely on features of the R packages they use have no exact equivalents in Python.
]

#### Compustat (`comp`)

Compustat is the most common source of financial-statement data for academic research, particulary for US firms.
Academic researchers generally get Compustat data through WRDS.

While Compustat is a rich source of data from income statement, balance sheets, and cash flow statements, its direct use by @bali2016 is limited to calculating the book value of common equity.
The table from Compustat needed for this purpose is `comp.funda`, which supplies annual data.

More on Compustat can be found in [Chapter 6](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/fin-state.html) and [Chapter 8](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/fin-state-reprise.html) of @GowDing2024.

While @bali2016 make little use of Compustat data, many studies of the cross-section of stock returns go deeper into financial statements.
[Chapter 14](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/pead.html#post-earnings-announcement-drift) of @GowDing2024 covers @bernardThomas1989, which uses quarterly income before extraordinary items (`ibq` in `comp.fundq`) to measure earnings surprises, then compare abnormal returns across earnings-surprise deciles after the announcements.
[Chapter 15](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/accruals.html#accrual-anomaly) of @GowDing2024 focuses on @sloan1996, which uses annual financial statements (`comp.funda`) to separate earnings into accrual and cash-flow components, then compares subsequent returns across portfolios sorted on accruals.

#### CRSP (`crsp`)

The primary source of data in @bali2016 is the CRSP database.
According to its website, "the Center for Research in Security Prices, LLC (CRSP) maintains the most comprehensive collection of security price, return, and volume data for the NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stock markets.
Additional CRSP files provide stock indices, beta-based and cap-based portfolios, treasury bond and risk-free rates, mutual funds, and real estate data.
[CRSP] maintains the most comprehensive collection of security price, return, and volume data for the NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stock markets.
Additional CRSP files provide stock indices, beta-based and cap-based portfolios, treasury bond and risk-free rates, mutual funds, and real estate data."

According to [WRDS,](https://go.unimelb.edu.au/7cd8) "CRSP contains end-of-day and month-end prices on all listed NYSE, Amex, and NASDAQ common stocks along with basic market indices, and includes the most comprehensive distribution information available, with the most accurate total return calculations."

In 2022, CRSP introduced a new data format called *CIZ*.^[For more on CIZ, see the [CIZ database guide](https://indexes.morningstar.com/docs/guide/crsp-us-stock-databases-guide-for-flat-file-format-2-0?isRdp=true).]
The CIZ format replaced the *SIZ* format available when @bali2016 was written.
CRSP stopped releasing SIZ format data in early 2025, so no data on returns and stock prices are available in the SIZ format for periods after 2024.

One major change with CIZ was to the layout of the tables, with CIZ tables often being much larger because they contain data from what were multiple tables in SIZ.^[
    My local Parquet extract of the CIZ table `crsp.dsf_v2` is 4.63 GB, about 2.1 times the size of the 2.21 GB extract of the SIZ table `crsp.dsf`.
    The CIZ extract has 50 columns and the SIZ extract has 20.
]

A second change with CIZ affected the calculation of monthly returns.
With SIZ, monthly returns are calculated from month-end to month-end, with dividends reinvested at month-end.
In contrast, CIZ compounds daily returns over the month, with dividends reinvested on their ex-dividend dates.^[
    Of course, this is not necessary more "correct", as dividends can only be reinvested once they are received, which would be long after the ex-dividend date.
    To be sure, one could pledge one's claim to dividends to raise cash for reinvestment on the ex-dividend date, but there would be transaction costs and interest associated with this approach that the CRSP calculation ignores.
    Any calculation of returns that assumes that you can buy at the month-end price in one month and sell at the month-end price in another will always be an approximation of the returns that a hypothetical investor could actually earn.
]

A third change with CIZ was the incorporation of any applicable delisting returns into the reported monthly return.
In contrast, the SIZ data available to @bali2016 placed delisting returns in a separate table and researchers bore the burden of incorporating delisting returns, which were often missing from that table.
See [CRSP's comparison of the formats](https://www.crsp.org/crsp_pdf/crsp-us-stock-indexes-databases-siz-to-ciz-executive-summary/).

Because my focus here is on providing a reader's companion to @bali2016, I use the final vintage of the SIZ data throughout this version of the book.
Because the SIZ files I use come from a later CRSP vintage than used in BEM, the underlying data can still differ, though in practice not by much.
A later edition of this book may instead use CIZ data or provide a guide to how the analyses could be conducted using CIZ data.

Daily returns come from `crsp.dsf` and monthly returns from `crsp.msf`.
We use `crsp.msenames` for data on industries and the exchanges on which stocks are traded.
Delisting returns come from `crsp.msedelist` and index data from `crsp.msi`.

The final CRSP table we use is `crsp.ccmxpf_lnkused`.
CRSP provides PERMNO, its own "permanent identifier" for each security in its database.
Additionally, CRSP provides a company-level identifier, PERMCO, for each company.
[WRDS](https://go.unimelb.edu.au/7cd8) tells us that CRSP's goals in creating these identifiers are to allow "for clean and accurate backtesting, time-series and event studies, measurement of performance, accurate benchmarking, and securities analysis."
Howver, the firm identifier on Compustat is GVKEY and `crsp.ccmxpf_lnkused` provides a way to link CRSP data with the relevant Compustat records.
[Chapter 7](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/identifiers.html#sec-ccm) of @GowDing2024 explains how to link CRSP and Compustat.^[
    The chapter's worked example uses `crsp.ccmxpf_lnkhist`.
    [This comparison of the CRSP–Compustat link tables](https://gist.github.com/iangow/fca4cb10b048f5c798113da7039c2688) shows how to reconstruct `crsp.ccmxpf_lnkused` from `crsp.ccmxpf_lnkhist` apart from the `ulinkid` field.
]

#### Fama-French factors (`ff`)

I use two WRDS tables, `ff.factors_monthly` and `ff.factors_daily`, for the Fama–French factors and the risk-free rate in many of the analyses.
For example, the [beta chapter](beta-replication.qmd) uses the market excess return from both tables to estimate daily and monthly betas.

For some replications I use archived releases from [Kenneth French's Data Library](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library.html) to get closer to the factor vintages available when BEM prepared their book.
The [skewness](skewness-replication.qmd), [idiosyncratic volatility](volatility-replication.qmd), and [liquid samples](liquid-samples-replication.qmd) chapters use the June 2014 release.
The four-factor volatility model also uses the daily momentum series from that release.
[`eap_pl.get_ff_factors()`](eap_pl/reference/get_ff_factors.html) retrieves a specified vintage and keeps a checksum-verified local copy for later renders.

#### Source vintages

@tbl-data-vintages lists the inputs used in this build.
The source update date comes from the metadata embedded in each Parquet file, read with [db2pq](https://iangow.github.io/db2pq/).
It is not the sample end date or the date the file was downloaded.

::: {#data-vintages}
```{python}
#| label: tbl-data-vintages
#| tbl-cap: WRDS inputs and source update dates
#| code-fold: true

import re

from db2pq import pq_last_modified
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

tables = [
    ("comp", "funda", "Compustat",
     "Annual fundamentals for book equity."),
    ("crsp", "dsf", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Daily returns for beta estimation in @sec-bem-beta and daily prices, returns, and volume for @sec-liquidity-replication."),
    ("crsp", "msf", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Legacy prices, shares outstanding, and monthly returns."),
    ("crsp", "msenames", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Historical share codes, exchanges, and industries."),
    ("crsp", "msedelist", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "Delisting returns and codes for monthly holding-period returns."),
    ("crsp", "msi", "CRSP legacy (SIZ)",
     "CRSP value-weighted index for the market factor comparison."),
    ("crsp", "ccmxpf_lnkused", "CRSP/Compustat Merged",
     "Historical links from Compustat firms to CRSP securities."),
    ("ff", "factors_monthly", "Fama–French",
     "Monthly factors and the risk-free rate for betas, alphas, and market checks."),
    ("ff", "factors_daily", "Fama–French",
     "Daily market excess returns for the crash checks in @sec-bem7-market and for estimating daily betas."),
]

rows = [
    "| WRDS table | Dataset | Used for | Source updated |",
    "|:---|:---|:---|:---|",
]
for schema, name, dataset, purpose in tables:
    metadata = pq_last_modified(name, schema) or ""
    match = re.search(r"Updated (\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2})", metadata)
    updated = match[1] if match else "Not recorded"
    rows.append(f"| `{schema}.{name}` | {dataset} | {purpose} | {updated} |")

display(Markdown("\n".join(rows)))
```
:::

#### Create the Parquet repository {#sec-create-data-repository}

[]{#create-data-repository}Copy `.env.example` to `.env` in the book checkout and set `DATA_DIR` to your Parquet root and `WRDS_ID` to your WRDS username.
After `uv sync`, run the setup script from that checkout.
If you already have the source files there, you can skip this step.
If your WRDS account lacks access to the legacy CRSP tables, use licensed SIZ extracts at the corresponding paths.
`eap_pl.load_parquet()` reads these files from `DATA_DIR/schema/table.parquet`.

```sh
uv run scripts/download_wrds_tables.py
```

The following Python example shows how the script uses `db2pq.wrds_update_pq()` to export the WRDS tables to `DATA_DIR`.

```python
from db2pq import wrds_update_pq
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

tables = {
    "crsp": ["msf", "dsf", "msenames", "msedelist", "msi", "ccmxpf_lnkused"],
    "comp": ["funda"],
    "ff": ["factors_monthly", "factors_daily"],
}

for schema, names in tables.items():
    for name in names:
        wrds_update_pq(name, schema)
```

### Other data sources {#other-inputs}

The annual methods chapters construct December betas, size, and book-to-market from the local source data when needed.
See Chapters [-@sec-bem-beta], [-@sec-size-replication], and [-@sec-value-replication] for how each measure is constructed.
The monthly replications estimate the 12-month daily beta on demand with [`eap_pl.load_monthly_betas()`](eap_pl/reference/load_monthly_betas.html).
See the [render instructions](https://github.com/iangow/eap_py#render).

The size builder and the [CRSP](crsp-replication.qmd) and [Value](value-replication.qmd) chapters use the [BLS all-items CPI for urban consumers, not seasonally adjusted](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCNS), from FRED, to express market capitalizations in December 2012 dollars.
This file does not come from WRDS.

@sec-liquidity-replication uses the December 2013 Pástor–Stambaugh liquidity release bundled with `eap_pl`.

## Winsorization and Truncation

**Winsorization** caps values outside chosen percentile cutoffs at the corresponding cutoff.
**Truncation** sets those values to missing, so analyses that require the variable exclude those observations.
In [Section 1.2](https://catalogimages.wiley.com/images/db/pdf/9781118095041.excerpt.pdf), @bali2016 describe both methods as ways to limit the influence of extreme values.
They suggest capping observations that still convey information about genuinely high or low values, and consider truncation when the extremes appear to come from a different process.
They urge caution when the conclusions depend on which treatment is used.

BEM compute the cutoffs separately for each year or month because they analyze each period's cross-section before summarizing the results over time.
Their 0.5% rule uses the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles.
In @sec-bem-correlation, both variables are winsorized for Pearson correlations, and Spearman correlations use ranks of the original values.
In @sec-bem-annual-fm, the regressors are winsorized and the excess-return outcome is used as observed.

I compute the winsorization cutoffs by linear interpolation with `.eap.winsorize(prob=0.005, quantile_method="linear")`.
The `eap_pl.winsorized_corr()` helper applies this rule to each variable after keeping pairs with two finite values.
In @sec-bem-beta, `.over("month")` computes cutoffs separately for each month's beta estimates.
I then fit the Fama–MacBeth regressions with `statspai.fama_macbeth()`.

For examples of winsorization and truncation and a comparison with robust regression, see [Chapter 24 of *Empirical Research in Accounting*](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/extreme-vals.html#sec-leone).

## Newey and West (1987) Adjustment

In Section 1.3, @bali2016 explain why inference on a time-series mean can be sensitive to changing variance and correlation across periods.
Regressing a series on a constant gives its sample mean as the intercept.
The adjustment of @neweywest1987 estimates the standard error using covariances across periods, with less weight on more distant lags.
Depending on the pattern of autocorrelation, the adjustment can increase or decrease the standard error.
In @sec-bem-portfolio-analysis, BEM use the adjustment for average portfolio returns and spreads, and in time-series factor regressions for portfolio alphas.

For Fama–MacBeth regressions, BEM apply the adjustment to the sequence of estimated coefficients, with one estimate per cross-section.
BEM motivate six lags with a rule of thumb for a series of about 600 monthly observations and also use six lags in their annual example, which has only 24 coefficient estimates.
@gow2010 call this procedure FM-NW and find that its standard errors can remain too small when the underlying panel has both cross-sectional and time-series dependence.
A short coefficient series provides limited information about persistence in the underlying data [@gow2010, p. 488].

The annual, beta, size, and book-to-market regressions replicated here use realized excess returns over nonoverlapping holding periods.
This resembles the return-based application in @gow2010 [sec. V], where shared shocks across stocks are the main concern.
For slope inference, the relevant serial dependence involves the joint behavior of regressors and residuals.
Size is highly persistent in my replications.
Across specifications, the pooled lag-one correlations between residuals for the same stock range from about $-0.05$ to $-0.01$.

For every slope in the monthly replications, the ordinary and six-lag tests agree at the 5% level.
@sec-annual-fm-inference shows how the adjustment changes inference on size in the annual example.

For more on Newey–West, Fama–MacBeth, and clustering, see Section 5.6 of *Empirical Research in Accounting* in the [StatsPAI edition](https://iangow.github.io/era_statpai/stat-inf.html#sec-dependence) or the [Polars edition](https://iangow.github.io/era_pl_book/stat-inf.html#sec-dependence).

## Python packages

### Polars

I use Polars, imported as `pl`, to filter, join, and summarize the data throughout the book.
A `DataFrame` holds the data in memory, and a `LazyFrame` describes a query that runs when I call `.collect()`.
Expressions such as `pl.col("ret")` refer to columns, and `.over("month")` applies a calculation separately within each month.
See the [Polars user guide](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/).

### `eap_pl`

Here `eap` stands for "Empirical Asset Pricing" and `pl` is the standard abbreviation for Polars.
The `eap_pl` package was created specifically for this reader's companion and streamlines work that recurs across chapters, including reading local Parquet tables, constructing stock-level variables, and forming portfolios.

Importing `eap_pl` also registers the `.eap` namespace for Polars expressions and DataFrames.
For example, `.eap.winsorize()` clips an expression at quantile cutoffs.
For more details, see the [`eap_pl` function reference](eap_pl/reference/index.html).

### Great Tables

I use Great Tables to format the book's tables, usually through `.eap.show_table()` on a Polars DataFrame.
For tables that need grouped rows or spanning column headings, I use Great Tables methods through `.style`, as in the [table of beta portfolio alphas and factor loadings](portfolio-analysis.qmd#tbl-bem5-risk-adjusted).
See the [Great Tables documentation](https://posit-dev.github.io/great-tables/).

### `plotnine_polars`

I use `plotnine_polars` for all figures in the book.
The figures build on the grammar of graphics popularized in R by Hadley Wickham’s [`ggplot2`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/).
Hassan Kibirige and the other contributors have done an excellent job bringing that approach to Python with [`plotnine`](https://plotnine.org/).

I wrote `plotnine_polars` to give `plotnine` a more fluent interface for use with Polars.
It adds `.ggplot()` to Polars DataFrames so I can build a figure by chaining methods for aesthetics, layers, scales, and labels.
The figures on the [composition of the CRSP sample](crsp-replication.qmd#sec-bem7-composition) show how this works with time series grouped by exchange or industry.
I first explored this style in my note [*Making `plotnine` more ‘Pythonic’*](https://iangow.github.io/notes/plotnine_test/plotnine_testone.html).
See the [`plotnine_polars` documentation](https://iangow.github.io/plotnine_polars/).

For a broader introduction to data visualization, I recommend Kieran Healy’s [*Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction*](https://socviz.co/).
I translated his examples using `plotnine_polars` in [*Data Visualization: A Python/Polars Companion*](https://iangow.github.io/socviz-polars/).

### StatsPAI

I use StatsPAI (`statspai`) to estimate regressions and calculate standard errors.
For example, `statspai.fama_macbeth()` fits a cross-sectional regression in each period, averages the coefficients over time, and can apply a Newey–West adjustment to the standard errors of those averages.
The [Fama–MacBeth chapter](annual-regressions.qmd) shows this for annual data.
See the [StatsPAI project page](https://github.com/brycewang-stanford/StatsPAI).
